rules.title: Creating a player character
rules.summary: Generate abilities using the method your DM permits, then choose race, class and alignment and record languages, money, equipment and hit points.
bullets: Keep a character record with possessions, spells and cumulative XP.
Race and class eligibility must be checked before choices are finalized.

rules.title: The six ability scores
rules.summary: Strength, intelligence, wisdom, dexterity, constitution and charisma describe different capabilities. The DM chooses the method used to generate them.
bullets: Ability requirements can restrict race or class choices.
Consult each ability's own adjustments rather than applying a universal modifier.

rules.title: Strength and exceptional strength
rules.summary: Strength affects melee accuracy, damage, carrying allowance and forcing obstacles. Fighters with strength 18 roll percentile dice for exceptional strength.
bullets: The exceptional-strength table is restricted to fighters in this PHB rule.
Fighters with strength 16 or higher receive a 10% earned-XP bonus.

Weight allowance adjusts the normal unencumbered allowance, measured in gold-piece weight (10 gp = 1 lb). Parenthesized door chances are out of six for fighters forcing locked, barred, magically held or wizard-locked doors: only one attempt per door is allowed. Bend-bars/lift-gates attempts are also one-time attempts.

rules.title: Intelligence and learning spells
rules.summary: Intelligence limits a magic-user's spell levels and spells known. Learning checks use percentile dice against the applicable chance-to-know entry.
bullets: A successful check determines whether the spell can be learned when found.
The minimum-spells rule permits rechecking failed spells until the minimum is met.
Stop learning in that spell-level group when the maximum is reached.
Additional languages by Intelligence: 3–7: 0; 8–9: 1; 10–11: 2; 12–13: 3; 14–15: 4; 16: 5; 17: 6; 18: 7. Nonhuman language rules and racial limits also apply.

Magic-user spell learning rows are Intelligence: chance to know each listed spell / minimum spells per spell level / maximum spells per spell level: 9: 35%/4/6; 10–12: 45%/5/7; 13–14: 55%/6/9; 15–16: 65%/7/11; 17: 75%/8/14; 18: 85%/9/18; 19 or more: 95%/10/all.
Minimum Intelligence to use magic-user spells of levels 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 is respectively 10, 12, 14, 16 and 18.

rules.title: Wisdom: bonus spells and spell failure
rules.summary: Wisdom's clerical bonus spells are cumulative, but become available only when the cleric can already cast that spell level. Low wisdom can cause spell failure.
bullets: The magical-attack adjustment applies to mental attacks involving willpower, not every saving throw.
A failed clerical spell is expended with no effect.
Magical-attack saving-throw adjustment by Wisdom: 3 −3; 4 −2; 5–7 −1; 8–14 none; 15 +1; 16 +2; 17 +3; 18 +4. This applies to mental attack forms involving will force.

Cleric bonus spell increments and failure chance by Wisdom: 9 none/20%; 10 none/15%; 11 none/10%; 12 none/5%; 13 one 1st-level/0%; 14 one 1st-level/0%; 15 one 2nd-level/0%; 16 one 2nd-level/0%; 17 one 3rd-level/0%; 18 one 4th-level/0%. Bonus increments accumulate and require access to the spell level. Wisdom 17 is the minimum for 6th-level cleric spells and 18 for 7th-level spells.

rules.title: Dexterity: surprise, missiles and defense
rules.summary: Dexterity has separate reaction/attacking and defensive adjustments, plus a separate table for thief functions.
bullets: The reaction/attacking adjustment applies to surprise and missile attacks.
Defensive benefits depend on being able to react or dodge; use the applicable combat rules.
Add relevant racial thief adjustments to the ability adjustments.
Dexterity rows are score: reaction/missile attack adjustment / defensive adjustment: 3 −3/+4; 4 −2/+3; 5 −1/+2; 6 0/+1; 7–14 0/0; 15 0/−1; 16 +1/−2; 17 +2/−3; 18 +3/−4.

Thief Dexterity adjustments, in percentage points for pick pockets/open locks/find-remove traps/move silently/hide in shadows: 9 −15/−10/−10/−20/−10; 10 −10/−5/−10/−15/−5; 11 −5/0/−5/−10/0; 12 0/0/0/−5/0; 13–15 0/0/0/0/0; 16 0/+5/0/0/0; 17 +5/+10/0/+5/+5; 18 +10/+15/+5/+10/+10. Apply these to base chances; racial adjustments are additional.

rules.title: Constitution and hit points
rules.summary: Apply the constitution hit-point adjustment to each hit die; a penalty cannot reduce a die below 1 hit point.
bullets: Under this PHB rule, only fighters, including paladins and rangers, receive constitution bonuses above +2 per die.
System shock and resurrection survival are different percentage checks.

The initial Constitution score caps the number of raise-dead or resurrection revivifications, and each such revivification reduces Constitution by 1. Increasing or restoring Constitution does not raise that original limit. The text notes that other magic such as wish may provide another means.

rules.title: Resurrection survival and lifetime limit
rules.summary: The initial constitution score limits the number of times a character can be raised or resurrected. Each revival also reduces constitution by 1.
bullets: Magically improving constitution does not replenish that original lifetime limit.

rules.title: Race, class eligibility and level limits
rules.summary: The PHB offers dwarf, elf, gnome, half-elf, halfling, half-orc and human characters. Racial tables restrict classes and, for many non-human classes, advancement.
bullets: Your DM may restrict available races for the campaign.
UA provides additional racial choices and revised limits; keep the selected source explicit.

PHB class level table (U = unlimited; parenthesized entries are non-player characters only; omitted classes are unavailable to that race): dwarf fighter 9, thief U, assassin 9, cleric (8); elf fighter 7, magic-user 11, thief U, assassin 10, cleric (7); gnome fighter 6, illusionist 7, thief U, assassin 8, cleric (7); half-elf cleric 5, druid U, fighter 8, ranger 8, magic-user 8, thief U, assassin 11; halfling fighter 6, thief U, druid (6); half-orc cleric 4, fighter 10, thief 8, assassin U; human all listed classes U. All are still subject to applicable ability and class requirements.

PHB fighter limits by Strength: dwarf below 17 → 7, at 17 → 8, otherwise maximum 9; elf below 17 → 5, at 17 → 6, otherwise maximum 7; gnome below 18 → 5, otherwise 6; half-elf below 17 → 6, at 17 → 7, otherwise 8. Halfling Hairfeet and others under Strength 17 → 4; Tallfellows at 17 and Stouts at 18 → 5; Tallfellows with 18 → 6.

PHB magic-user limits by Intelligence: elf below 17 → 9, at 17 → 10, otherwise maximum 11; half-elf below 17 → 6, at 17 → 7, otherwise maximum 8. Gnome illusionists with Intelligence or Dexterity below 17 are limited to 5; with both 17 to 6; otherwise table maximum 7. Half-orc thieves with Dexterity below 17 are limited to 6, at 17 to 7, otherwise maximum 8.
The printed half-elven ranger 8 entry bears footnote 4, but that footnote explicitly describes half-elven fighters. The table’s application of that footnote to rangers is unresolved.

rules.title: Humans changing class
rules.summary: A human may stop advancing in one profession and begin another, subject to ability and alignment requirements. This differs from simultaneous non-human multiclassing.

Once the new level exceeds the old, class functions may be combined subject to equipment restrictions.

rules.title: Armor class and magical protection
rules.summary: Armor and shields establish a base AC, with dexterity and magic modifying it. Lower numeric armor classes offer better protection.
bullets: Unarmored is AC 10; plate mail with a shield is AC 2 in this table.
Each +1 of magic armor or shield decreases AC by 1.
A monster's AC may represent hide, agility or other defenses rather than worn armor.
Base AC without shield: leather or padded 8; studded leather or ring mail 7; scale 6; chain 5; splint or banded 4; plate 3.
A shield improves these listed armor classes by one when applicable; shield alone is AC 9.

rules.title: Wandering and placed encounters
rules.summary: Wandering encounters occur through encounter checks; placed encounters arise from the DM's keyed locations. Unnecessary time and noise can attract more danger.
bullets: Wandering monsters often offer little treasure compared with the resources spent fighting them.
Negotiation or avoidance can be useful alternatives to combat.

In that encounter procedure, men-at-arms accompany parties on dungeon levels 1–3; on level 4 or deeper the companions are henchmen. Character-class incompatibilities and per-party class maxima must also be applied using the source table.

rules.title: Encounter reaction checks
rules.summary: For a creature capable of conversation, the DM can roll percentile dice and adjust for charisma and applicable loyalty factors to determine its reaction.
bullets: Adjusted percentile 01 or less–05: violently hostile, immediate attack; 06–25: hostile, immediate action. Either can call for a morale check if appropriate.

Circumstances and the creatures involved still matter; a reaction check is not guaranteed cooperation.

rules.title: Morale and losing the will to fight
rules.summary: Morale checks can govern non-leader NPCs, hirelings, henchmen and intelligent opponents. Casualties, lost leadership and superior enemy force can trigger checks.
bullets: Check each round against an obviously superior force. Apply +5% at 25% party casualties, +10% if the leader is unconscious, +15% at 50% or more casualties, and +30% if the leader is slain or deserts; the casualty thresholds also apply to individual wounds.

Modifiers: each enemy deserting −5%, each enemy slain −10%, inflicting casualties without receiving any −20%, each friend killed +10%, taking casualties without inflicting any +10%, each friend deserting +15%, and being outnumbered and outclassed at least 3 to 1 +20%.
Roll percentile dice against the creature’s morale or loyalty score after adjustments; the amount by which the adjusted roll exceeds the score determines the failure outcome.
Failure by 1–15% means fall back fighting; 16–30% disengage and retreat; 31–50% flee in panic; 51% or more surrender.

rules.title: Comeliness is separate from charisma
rules.summary: UA adds comeliness for physical appearance and initial reactions. Charisma still governs the longer-term interpersonal relationship once a character is known.
bullets: Roll 3d6 for base comeliness after the first six abilities. Charisma modifiers: below 3 −8; 3 −5; 4–5 −3; 6–8 −1; 9–12 0; 13–15 +1; 16–17 +2; 18 +3; above 18 +5. Later gains or losses of charisma adjust comeliness point for point.

Racial adjustment applies to reactions from other races: half-orc −3; dwarf or gnome −1; halfling or human 0; half-elf or sylvan elf +1; gray or high elf +2. Treat each starred pair as the same race for this purpose.

The following reaction bands concern creatures of human sort. At −16 or below, viewers recoil, flee or may attack; if viewer and subject are both evil, treat the score as positive. At −15 to −9, viewers show disgust and hostility; if all are evil, the negative score can be regarded as positive. At −8 to 0, viewers feel aversion and may become openly hostile.

At 1–6, viewers tend toward unease; enough conversation can let charisma offset it. At 7–9, the initial reaction is negative but high charisma can quickly overcome it. At 10–13, appearance has no effect on the viewer.
At 14–17, initial reaction improves by a percentage equal to the score; members of the opposite sex are affected as by fascination unless their Wisdom exceeds half the score.

At 18–21, initial reaction improves by 150% of the score. Opposite-sex viewers are affected as by fascination unless Wisdom exceeds two-thirds the score; same-sex viewers are similarly affected unless Wisdom is at least half the score. Harsh rejection can cause the rejected individual to react as if the subject had negative comeliness equal to half the positive score.

At 22–25, the reaction adjustment is twice the score. Fascination affects those with Wisdom less than two-thirds of the score; a consciously sought opposite-sex individual is fascinated unless Wisdom is 18 or higher. Harsh rejection has the same effect as in the 18–21 band.

At 26–30, reserved for unusual extraplanar demigods or deities, the reaction adjustment is twice the score. Fascination applies except to those with Wisdom at least 75% of the score, and Wisdom 19 or higher always permits a saving throw. A consciously sought opposite-sex individual is affected unless Wisdom is 20 or higher.

Fascination allows a saving throw versus spell; nonmagical comeliness fascination is not removed by dispel magic or antimagic. A fascinated creature follows an order if 3d6 does not exceed the subject’s comeliness: add 1 to the roll for requests against its interest, up to +6 or more for hazardous requests; a higher roll breaks fascination. Treatment during fascination affects subsequent reaction.

Comeliness is temporary as a reaction factor: once the subject is known, use charisma. Fascination does not prevent fighting or spellcasting or make the subject a puppet. Change self and alter self adjust comeliness by at most 1 point; an illusion of a high-comeliness creature works for one round; polymorph changes it by 2 points; shapechange gives the final form’s full effect.

rules.title: UA weapon specialization
rules.summary: Fighters and rangers can choose weapon specialization at creation. It normally uses two proficiency slots; a non-crossbow bow requires an additional slot.
bullets: Only fighters and rangers may specialize, choosing at character creation. Specialization costs two proficiency slots; a non-crossbow bow requires one additional slot. The weapon must be a specific type.
Melee specialization grants +1 to hit and +2 damage in addition to applicable Strength and magic bonuses. Other missile weapons also grant +1 to hit and +2 damage.

Bow point blank is 6–30 feet: +2 to hit and damage and double damage on a hit; the source gives 6–16 damage for a nonmagical arrow, plus applicable Strength or magic bonuses. At short range, beginning at 30 feet up to the lower limit of medium range, the specialist gains +1 to hit and damage. A nocked and drawn bow with target in sight may fire before initiative.

Crossbow point blank is 6–60 feet: +2 to hit and damage and double damage, with a 6–12 nonmagical light-crossbow example excluding Strength or magic bonuses. At short range gain +1 to hit and damage; at medium gain +1 to hit with no specialization damage bonus. A cocked and aimed crossbow with target in range gains a shot before initiative.

Specialist attacks per round at levels 1–6 / 7–12 / 13+: melee 3/2, 2/1, 5/2; bow 2/1, 3/1, 4/1; light crossbow 1/1, 3/2, 2/1; heavy crossbow 1/2, 1/1, 3/2; lasso or staff sling 1/1, 3/2, 2/1; thrown dagger 3/1, 4/1, 5/1; thrown dart 4/1, 5/1, 6/1; other missiles or hurled weapons 3/2, 2/1, 5/2. The table supersedes ordinary fighter/ranger attacks for the specialized weapon.

Double specialization costs another proficiency slot when a character qualifies for a new weapon, and must be in the weapon already specialized in. Only melee weapons qualify, excluding pole arms and the two-handed sword; it gives +3 to hit and +3 damage with that weapon.
Specialization hit bonuses are not magical and do not affect creatures hit only by magical weapons; applicable magical weapon bonuses are additional.

rules.title: Apply racial ability adjustments in order
rules.summary: A non-human or part-human character must meet the race's ability minimums. Apply racial bonuses and penalties before enforcing the race's maximum scores.
bullets: Minimums may be met by the initial roll plus the race's permitted bonus.

PHB racial ability limits below show each ability as minimum–maximum. A maximum written M/F gives the male maximum first and female maximum second; otherwise both are the same. Apply racial adjustments before the maximum; qualifying minimums can include an applicable racial bonus.
Dwarf: Strength 8–18/17; Intelligence 3–18; Wisdom 3–18; Dexterity 3–17; Constitution 12–19; Charisma 3–16.
Elf: Strength 3–18/16; Intelligence 8–18; Wisdom 3–18; Dexterity 7–19; Constitution 6–18; Charisma 8–18.
Gnome: Strength 6–18/15; Intelligence 7–18; Wisdom 3–18; Dexterity 3–18; Constitution 8–18; Charisma 3–18.
Half-elf: Strength 3–18/17; Intelligence 4–18; Wisdom 3–18; Dexterity 6–18; Constitution 6–18; Charisma 3–18.
Halfling: Strength 6–17/14; Intelligence 6–18; Wisdom 3–17; Dexterity 8–18; Constitution 10–19; Charisma 3–18.
Half-orc: Strength 6–18; Intelligence 3–17; Wisdom 3–14; Dexterity 3–17; Constitution 13–19; Charisma 3–12.

The PHB notes that fighters of all races might qualify for exceptional Strength; see the Strength table. This table covers the six listed nonhuman and part-human races; class requirements remain separate.
The dwarf Charisma maximum applies with respect to non-dwarves; the half-orc maximum applies with respect to non-orcs and non-half-orcs (PHB p.13).

rules.title: Duergar player-character defenses
rules.summary: UA gray dwarves keep dwarven magic-save bonuses and are unaffected by illusions, paralysis and poisons of magical or alchemical origin.

They speak dwarvish, undercommon and their alignment language, plus at most two other languages regardless of Intelligence.
If psionics are used, duergar have twice the usual chance of being psionic: double the Intelligence, Wisdom and Charisma bonuses; this does not guarantee psionic ability.

Gray dwarves can be fighters, clerics or thieves; thieves may be assassins or thief-acrobats. The listed multiclass options are fighter/cleric, fighter/thief, cleric/thief and cleric/assassin. PCs may be of any alignment.

A PC deep gnome is surprised only 1 in 12; it surprises others 9 in 10 when alone or with other deep gnomes and not wearing bulky armor.
Deep underground, it has a 60% chance to camouflage itself against natural rock, remaining effectively invisible until moving, attacking or taking another action that negates invisibility.
In melee against drow and kuo-toa, it gains +1 to hit and damage.
UA describes player-character deep gnomes as male; they may use the classes and class combinations available to surface gnomes.
They use standard gnomish abilities for detecting underground slopes and unsafe walls, and determining underground depth and direction.

They speak their own tongue and may learn other languages according to Intelligence. PCs cannot automatically converse with Elemental Plane of Earth creatures unless they have learned the relevant language, and are as likely to be attacked by them as other races.
Against attacks from giants, bugbears, ogre magi, ogres, trolls or titans, they receive the same benefits as surface gnomes. The underlying surface-gnome rule remains a separate reference.

rules.title: Gray, wood and wild elf distinctions
rules.summary: UA elven sub-races retain many high-elf traits but add specific changes. Gray elves gain +1 intelligence, potentially reaching 19.
bullets: Gray elves share high-elf abilities, including sleep and charm resistance, sword and bow ability, infravision, secret/concealed-door detection and silent movement when alone. They share high-elf languages and add +1 to the initial Intelligence roll, up to 19.

Wood (sylvan) elves have similar elven traits, gain +1 initial Strength (maximum 18) and −1 initial Intelligence. Their starting languages are elvish, common, treant and the tongue of woodland mammals; the passage gives them no other starting languages.

Wild elves (grugach) retain standard elven resistance, weapon bonuses, infravision, silent movement and door detection. They gain +2 initial Strength (maximum 18), deal with woodland creatures as if animal friendship were in effect, and set pits, snares and natural traps with a 90% success chance. Most speak only elvish, though a player character may also know some common.

The UA p.7 class table permits gray elves to be cavaliers, clerics, druids, fighters, rangers, magic-users or thieves (including acrobats and assassins); wood elves have those choices except cavalier; wild elves can be druids, fighters or thieves (including acrobats and assassins). Wild elf multiclassing is restricted to fighter/thief.
These are the UA class choices; ability requirements, multiclass rules and the separate UA class-level limits still apply. Do not merge them with the PHB-only class limits.

UA level-limit table conventions: use Wisdom for cleric/druid, Strength for fighter/ranger/assassin, Intelligence for magic-user, and Dexterity for thief; additional ability requirements appear in footnotes. U means unlimited for the appropriate race/class, subject to the highest level attainable by the class. Below the first score shown, use the lowest listed level; scores above the table do not raise its maximum. If single-classed and that class is an available multiclass choice for the character, the limit may be exceeded by 2. Class eligibility still applies.
UA elf cleric (all except dark elves): Wisdom 12–15: 7; 16: 8; 17: 9; 18: 10; 19: 11; 20–21: 12. Wild elves are not eligible for cleric under UA p.7.

UA elf druid: wild elf Wisdom 12–17: 10; 18: 11 and 19: 12, both requiring Charisma 18; 20: 14 and 21: 17, both requiring Charisma 19. The 12–17 rows have no additional Charisma footnote; normal class requirements still apply. Other elves: U, where class-eligible.

UA elf fighter: Strength 12–17 gives gray/high 5, wild 7, wood 6; 18 gives 6/8/7; 18/75 gives 7/8/8; 18/90 gives 8/10/9; 18/99 gives 9/11/10; 18/00 gives 10/12/11; 19 gives 11/13/12; 20 gives 11/13/14. Values in each group are gray/high, wild, wood respectively.
UA elf magic-user: Intelligence 17–18 gives gray 11 and wood 9; 19 gives 12/10; 20 gives 13/11; 21 gives 15/13; 22 gives 18/13. Wild elves cannot be magic-users under UA p.7.

UA elf thief is U. UA elf assassin: Strength 18, 18/01, 18/51 or 18/76 gives level 10; 18/99 gives 11 with Intelligence 18 and Wisdom 19; 18/00, 19 or 20 gives 12 with Intelligence 19 or Wisdom 19. Apply eligibility separately.

UA elf ranger: Strength 18 gives level 6; 18/01 gives 7 with Intelligence 15 and Wisdom 15, or 8 if both exceed 15; 18/51 gives 9 with Intelligence and Wisdom 16; 18/76, 18/99 or 18/00 gives 10 with Intelligence and Wisdom 17; 19 gives 12 and 20 gives 14, both requiring Intelligence and Wisdom 18. Wild elves cannot be rangers under UA p.7.

rules.title: Secondary skills are an optional background tool
rules.summary: A campaign may assign a secondary trade or craft to player characters and, if desired, henchmen. Assign it randomly or select it to suit the campaign's background. The skill gives limited practical knowledge judged by the DM.
bullets: An armorer might judge the quality of normal armor, repair chain links, or perhaps fashion certain weapons.
This procedure does not supply a universal proficiency-check system.
Random percentile: 01–02 armorer; 03–04 bowyer/fletcher; 05–10 farmer/gardener; 11–14 fisher (netting); 15–20 forester; 21–23 gambler; 24–27 hunter/fisher (hook and line).

28–32 husbandman (animal husbandry); 33–34 jeweler/lapidary; 35–37 leather worker/tanner; 38–39 limner/painter; 40–42 mason/carpenter; 43–44 miner; 45–46 navigator (fresh or salt water); 47–49 sailor (fresh or salt); 50–51 shipwright (boats or ships).

52–54 tailor/weaver; 55–57 teamster/freighter; 58–60 trader/barterer; 61–64 trapper/furrier; 65–67 woodworker/cabinetmaker; 68–85 no skill of measurable worth; 86–00 roll twice, ignoring that result thereafter.
At 1st level, the class is assumed to have been the character's main prior profession. Secondary skills reflect minor mundane training picked up earlier or incidentally.

The prose says to roll to determine whether a second skill is known and, on a 'TWO SKILLS' result, assign an appropriate second skill. The 86–00 table entry is worded 'ROLL TWICE IGNORING THIS RESULT HEREAFTER'.
Other examples of secondary-skill use include judging an item's general worth and soundness, finding food, making small repairs, and constructing crude items. These are examples for DM adjudication.
To judge a skill's extent, consider what someone who knows only a little about the subject could do; use that as a scale for the character's secondary skill.

Non-intelligent pursuers have a 100% probability. If the chance is under 100%, roll d10 again to test it; success distracts them for one round.

Treasure can distract pursuers of low intelligence or higher: start at 10%–100%, adding 10% per 10 items for low-intelligence pursuers or 10% per 100 gp of value or potential value for those of average intelligence or more. Test with a second d10; success lasts one round or the time needed to collect the treasure, whichever is longer. Tiny valuables can go unnoticed.

rules.title: Items save according to material, exposure and magic
rules.summary: An item saving throw applies when the object is actually exposed to the attack. Use the material row and the specific attack form in the item matrix.
bullets: Magical items gain +2, plus another +1 for each enchantment plus above +1; a +2 item therefore gets +3.
An item gains +5 against attacks in its own mode, such as fire against a ring of fire resistance.
Normal fire, magical fire, fireball and electrical attack forms have distinct columns; do not substitute one general damage save.

Read each item sequence as the required d20 score or higher, in order: acid; crushing blow; normal blow; disintegration; fall; fireball or breath; magical fire; normal fire; magical frost; lightning bolt; electrical discharge/current. The table prints 0 and scores above 20; apply relevant adjustments.

Liquid covers potions, magical oils, poisons and acids while the container remains intact; soft metal or jewelry includes pearls. Mirror means silvered glass; use soft-metal or hard-metal rows for silver or steel mirrors.
Hard metal struck forcefully against a very hard surface after extreme cold takes −10 on the die. Nonmagical items also gain +5 against attacks in their own mode.
The fall column assumes a 5-foot fall onto a hard surface: softer wood-like surfaces give +1 and fleshy-soft surfaces +5; each additional 5 feet subtracts 1 from the saving die.
Normal fire requires sufficient exposure: examples give paper/parchment 1 melee round, cloth 2, bone/ivory 3. Other attack forms use the DMG p.80 definitions.

Acid assumes a considerable volume of strong acid or immersion long enough to affect the item. A crushing blow is a heavy impact; a normal blow is from a normal-strength opponent or a fairly heavy object. Disintegration is the magical effect.

Fireball includes a magical fireball, meteor swarm or red-dragon breath; magical fire includes wall of fire, fire storm and flame strike. Magical frost includes cold such as white-dragon breath, cone of cold or ice storm.
Lightning bolt includes magical lightning called from the sky or blue-dragon breath; electrical discharge/current includes electric-eel shock, magical items and traps.

rules.title: Overlapping potions can interact unpredictably
rules.summary: Check the potion-miscibility procedure when potions are physically mixed or when someone drinks another potion while a previous one is still active.
bullets: The DM makes the compatibility check secretly.
01: Explosion; internal damage 6–60 hp and those within 5″ take 1–10 hp. If mixed externally, all within 10 feet take 4–24 hp, no save.
02–03: Lethal poison kills the imbiber; if mixed externally, a 10-foot-diameter poison cloud requires those within to save versus poison or die.
04–08: Nausea and −1 strength and dexterity for 5–20 rounds, no save; one potion is cancelled and the other has half strength and duration, determined randomly.
09–15: Both potions are cancelled. 16–25: One randomly selected potion is cancelled and the other remains normal. 26–35: Both are at half efficacy.

36–90: Both work normally unless contradictory effects cancel. 91–99: One randomly selected potion has 150% efficacy, subject to the DM deciding whether effect and duration or only duration may increase.
00: One potion functions permanently on the imbiber; harmful side effects are possible.

progressionNote.text: The source says the progression is not even and a variable 5% increment appears at 19 and 20. It explains that this gives lower-level clerics a chance against tougher monsters and allows high-level clerics to destroy weaker undead. If an exact progression is needed, it says to follow levels 1, 2, and 3 and correct to the right; column 4 should read, top to bottom, T, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 20. rules.title: Druid Spell Components: Mistletoe, Holly, and Oak Leaves
rules.summary: Material-component quality changes druid spell effectiveness; druidic spells requiring a material component assume mistletoe gathered by the source method.
bullets: Mistletoe is the druids’ religious symbol; holly is of lesser importance, and oak leaves have some magical power. Druidic spells with a material component assume mistletoe gathered as described below.
Greater mistletoe is properly harvested by the druid: on Midsummer’s Eve, locate it, cut it with a gold or silver sickle, and catch it in a bowl before it touches the ground.
Lesser mistletoe was not harvested on the eve of Midsummer, or was taken in an unprescribed way such as picking it by hand.
Borrowed mistletoe is mistletoe not personally harvested by the druid.
Holly and oak leaves must be gathered by the druid, but may be picked or gathered in any manner.

rules.title: Appendix C party-size procedure
rules.summary: The source procedure generates two to five characters, then fills the group to nine with men-at-arms or henchmen.
bullets: Roll d4 and add 1 to get the number of characters (2–5).
Roll on the Character Subtable for each character profession; ignore contradictory results and any result above that profession’s per-party maximum.
Subtract the number of characters from 9 to get the number of accompanying men-at-arms or henchmen.

rules.title: Appendix C character-level procedure
rules.summary: The source gives a dungeon/monster-level rule through dungeon level 4, then a d6-based level and one-step adjustment procedure.
bullets: Through dungeon level 4, a character’s level equals the greater of the dungeon level or monster level.
Thereafter, determine a level from 7th through 12th by rolling d6 + 6.
If that total is above the dungeon level, reduce it by 1. If below, increase it by 1, but do not exceed 12 unless the dungeon level is 16th or deeper.

rules.title: Appendix C companions and henchmen
rules.summary: The source distinguishes men-at-arms from henchmen by dungeon level and gives class-compatibility, party-composition, and henchman-level guidance.
bullets: Men-at-arms accompany characters only on dungeon levels 1–3; at level 4 or deeper, the other party members are henchmen.
Determine henchman professions on the Character Subtable; ignore incompatible results. The printed examples include a paladin as a thief’s henchman and a ranger below 8th level with any henchman.
Pair each character with one or more henchmen in rotation until the party totals nine members.

The source describes each henchman’s level as one-third the master’s level, with its stated fractional rounding, plus 1 level per 3 levels of the master’s experience when the master is above 8th. It gives examples: a 5th-level master has a 2nd-level henchman; at 9th it prints “3 + 3” or 6th level; it says the bonus is 3 at 11th and 4 at 12th.
rules.notes: The conditional rounding wording and examples are preserved literally. The source does not specify an implementation for fractional rounding and the later bonus wording is underspecified; this proposal does not infer a correction or formula.
rules.uncertainties: The conditional rounding wording and examples are preserved literally. The source does not specify an implementation for fractional rounding and the later bonus wording is underspecified; this proposal does not infer a correction or formula.

rules.summary: Bounded guidance for generating abilities and alignment, equipping character levels and men-at-arms, and selecting cleric or magic-user spells.

Choose cleric and magic-user spells suited to the party while observing known-spell limits; henchmen with spell ability receive similarly selected spells.

rules.title: DMG p34 Sword-maker monthly output
rules.summary: Source table: Weapon-maker sword output exceptions.
bullets: A weapon maker is described as a smith-armorer specializing in high-quality arms. The source names three specialties: Bowyer-Arrowsmith-Fletcher; Swordsmith-Daggersmith; Weaponer General. Bowyers make bows including crossbows and their missiles; swordsmiths make swords and daggers; weaponers make arms not made by the other two.

Weapon makers require forge and workroom; apprentices are included in monthly cost. One is required for each 80 men or fraction. With free time, general output is one weapon/day after one-month start-up.

Composite and long bows instead require one-year start-up, then 2-5/month; heavy crossbows are 15/month; six sword rates appear in T23. All swords need scabbards made by a leather worker; a willing weapon maker is difficult to locate.

Ranger followers with the professed class of thief are always neutral good.

rules.title: Assassin guild follower generation, replacement, arrival, and timing
rules.summary: Assassin guild follower generation, replacement, arrival, and timing.
bullets: On attaining Guildmaster/Guildmistress status, roll 7d4 for lower-level assassins in the local guild; the DM may adjust for population. Determine race and level, then which stay; the source references the PHB 75% desertion rule. New additions to fill ranks are first level.

A separate passage states that the leader of all assassins (a nominal title at times) will have 28 followers: one 8th-level, two 7th-level, three 6th-level, four 5th-level, five 4th-level, six 3rd-level and seven 2nd-level assassins, plus 4-16 first-level followers. Mercenary fighters and men-at-arms are suggested, with a recommendation to develop henchmen after abilities are known.

If a player character displaces an NPC Grandfather/Grandmother of Assassins, followers are 75% likely to leave; the new leader may eventually attract up to 44 assassins under the new-guildmaster process.

Except when the followers arrive as a body, roll 1-30 using a d10 plus a d6 adjustment (1-2 no addition, 3-4 +10, 5-6 +20). The result gives the day after conditions are met when the first follower(s) appear. Further followers arrive at 1-8-day intervals. With no receiver, followers wait 1-4 days then depart forever; the character may designate a henchman or servant to receive them.

rules.title: Paladin warhorse acquisition, tenure, and loss of paladinhood
rules.summary: Paladin warhorse acquisition, tenure, and loss of paladinhood.
bullets: A paladin of 4th level or higher eventually calls for a warhorse, which appears as a magical sight/location rather than a physical arrival; the paladin must travel to it and gain it.

The journey is described as a rule of thumb of no more than seven days’ ride. Acquisition is not described as impossible: the mount may be wild or guarded by an evil fighter of the paladin’s level, with mortal combat as one possible route. The task may take days, possibly two or more weeks.

Once captured or won, the mount serves faithfully for ten years. Its intelligence is 5-7 points. Hit points per die are stated as never fewer than 50% of paladin level, excluding the additional +5; the source says a 16th-level paladin’s special steed has maximum hit points (8) per die, 5 × 8 = 40 + 5 additional hit points = 45 total hit points for 5 + 5 hit dice.
After ten years another mount is to be sought. If the character loses paladinhood, mount and rider have immutable enmity, the character cannot ride it, and it escapes at first opportunity.

rules.title: Spy mission categories and PC-versus-NPC resolution
rules.summary: Spy mission categories and PC-versus-NPC resolution.
bullets: Simple missions seek information about the general state of defenses, troop numbers or preparations for an activity; they rely on observation while the spy acts in a non-critical role among many people.
Difficult missions seek secret information or access/confidence and require active pursuit of the role.
Extraordinary missions are long, complex and hazardous, require insertion into an organization/operation and continuing detailed secret reports over a long association.

For player-character spies, resolution is interaction through the DM according to the player and situation; NPC spy missions use the success table. Source-described risk rises from simple to difficult to extraordinary.

rules.title: Spy discovery, precautions, failure, modifiers, and fanaticism
rules.summary: Spy discovery, precautions, failure, modifiers, and fanaticism.
bullets: Printed p18 discovery chance is cumulative 1% per day spent spying, capped at 10%, minus spy level, with a 1% minimum; precautions modify discovery.

Printed p19 separately supplies precaution-frequency categories and descriptions, leader/no-precautions treatment, and a tenfold discovery increase when another spy operates within 20-50 days after a spy is caught.

To test discovery, roll percentile dice for the stated time period; for a fraction, roll a third percentile die for tenths of a percent. The source example equates 1% per week to .14% per day and uses 99.9% for discovery on a one-day mission.

If discovered or the mission is unsuccessful, use the Spy Failure Table with the appropriate modifiers. Counterspies provide false information and follow the spy. Fanatical spies never turn double agent and kill themselves on a dice total over 60.
Do not combine the p18 per-day formula with p19 weekly/twice-weekly precaution percentages; the reviewed passage leaves their interaction unclear.

rules.title: Using Monster Treasure Types
rules.summary: Apply the Monster Manual’s treasure guidance with separate questions for Number Appearing, lair status, individual treasure, category rolls, and profile-specific instructions. A printed type code points to the p.105 lookup; it does not promise adventurers gain treasure by defeating a creature.
bullets: Treat Number Appearing as a good average-spread guideline and alter it for the adventure; it is not generally recommended for setting dungeon-level population.
Treat % IN LAIR as an encounter-location chance, separate from the probability printed in a treasure-table cell.
Away from its lair, a monster has no treasure unless it carries individual treasure or some form of magic.
Lair status may remain unknown until after the encounter is resolved.

Use a profile’s Treasure Type code to find the corresponding p.105 row. If individual treasure is indicated, each individual may carry or possibly carry the shown treasure; otherwise treasure is found only in lairs.
A lair encounter and an indicated Treasure Type do not by themselves guarantee that adventurers gain treasure by defeating the monster.
Roll the applicable treasure categories: listed contents are not guaranteed, and the lair may contain no wealth, including magic items.

Base treasure types on the mean number appearing. Adjust down for a few monsters; a minor increase may be appropriate when the group greatly exceeds the mean. Apply profile-specific instructions. The cited profiles are examples, not a complete census.
The source generally discourages using Treasure Types to determine treasure guarded by a creature in a dungeon.
Keep a parenthesized X 10 larger-hoard multiplier distinct from a separate Type X code. Preserve the printed notation.

spells.name: Animate Object

fields.Area: 1 cubic foot of solid material per level

effect: Animates one or more objects to attack the initially designated target. Any material can be animated.
conditions: Movement depends on means of propulsion and weight. Examples: a large stone pedestal rocks forward 1″ per round, a stone statue moves 4″ per round, a wooden statue 8″ per round, and a light ivory stool 12″ per round; slithering is about 1″–2″ per round and rolling 3″–6″ per round.

Light, supple objects can only obscure vision, obstruct movement, bind, trip or smother. Light, hard objects can strike for 1–2 hit points or possibly obstruct and trip as light, supple objects; hard medium-weight objects can crush or strike for 2–8 hit points, and larger/heavier objects for 3–12, 4–16 or 5–20 hit points.

Attack frequency depends on locomotion, appendages and method of attack, ranging from once every five melee rounds to once per melee round. Armor class depends on material and movement ability with regard to hitting. Damage suffered by the animated object depends on the weapon and material struck: sharp cutting weapons work well against fabric, leather or wood, while heavy smashing or crushing weapons work well against wood, stone or metal. The referee determines the object-specific factors and how much damage it can sustain before destruction.

spells.name: Find Familiar

fields.Saving throw: Special; summoned special familiars may resist
fields.Material: Brass brazier with charcoal, 100 gp of incense, herbs including basil/savory/catnip, and fat
fields.Special familiar benefits: Brownie (PHB p.66): the magic-user gains Dexterity equal to the brownie’s 18, is never surprised, and gains +2 on all saving throws. Pseudo-dragon (MM pp.79–80): a companion shares its 35% magic resistance while touching it; it uses limited telepathy and can convey sight and hearing to its companion within 24″. Imp or quasit familiar (MM pp.54, 80): telepathy shares the familiar’s senses up to one mile; within 1″ the master gains 25% magic resistance and regenerates 1 hit point per melee round. Within one mile the master gains one level of ability; at more than a mile the source says the character loses one level, and if the familiar is killed the character loses four levels. Once a week the familiar can contact a lower plane like commune with six questions.

effect: Call a familiar that can share senses, converse and serve as scout or guard; the caster cannot choose its kind.
A normal familiar has 2–4 HP and AC 7; while within 12″, its HP are added to its master's total.
conditions: The ritual may be attempted only once a year, and can produce no familiar.
Continue the incantation until the familiar arrives or the casting period ends.
The DM secretly determines the result.
exceptions: If a normal familiar dies, its master permanently loses twice that familiar’s hit points.
Special familiars have additional creature-specific rules; a successful resistance save leaves no familiar available that year.

Normal familiar table on d20: 1–4 black cat, 5–6 crow, 7–8 hawk, 9–10 screech owl, 11–12 toad, 13–14 weasel, 15 special, 16–20 no familiar. The printed adjustment subtracts 1 for each three caster levels and specifies a subsequent d16 roll in the stated circumstance.

For a special familiar, chaotic evil/neutral chaotic yields quasit; chaotic good/neutral/neutral good pseudo-dragon; lawful good/neutral lawful brownie; lawful evil/neutral evil imp. Selected familiar benefits are summarized in the special-familiar field; consult the Monster Manual for the creatures’ other abilities.

spells.name: Ceremony

fields.Materials: Holy symbol; additional requirements vary by religion

effect: The rite variant depends on the religion and leaves no lingering aura of magic, though an aura of good or evil may be present and detectable. The source lists coming of age, burial, and marriage at cleric level 1; dedication, investiture, and consecrate item at level 3; ordination and special vows at level 5; consecrate ground at level 7; and anathematize at level 9. Each requires a cleric of the indicated level or higher.

Coming of age grants a +1 bonus to one saving throw, usable at any time after the rite; in some cultures it marks entry to adulthood. Burial protects a corpse for one week as protection from evil; someone trying to disinter the body must save versus spell or stop and flee in fear for one turn. Marriage has no tangible after-effect and does not guarantee happiness or harmony, though it can carry moral or legal significance.

Dedication admits the recipient to the casting cleric’s religious ranks as a sanctioned worshiper; it is permanent unless the worshiper demonstrates a desire to change allegiance, in which case a higher-level cleric can replace it. Investiture must precede first-level cleric status. Ordination precedes service as a congregation priest or similar leader and is performed by a cleric of higher level than the recipient.

Consecrate item is performed on an object destined for an altar or another place in a religious edifice. Holy or unholy water used to keep it potent must be stored in a properly consecrated container.

Special vows are received by a would-be cavalier or paladin before beginning the chosen career. While they remain in effect, they protect against bestow curse spells but not cursed items; they also impose −4 on saving throws against a quest cast by a cleric of the same alignment as the caster of the vows. The vows may be renewed between levels or during advancement through the next level.

Consecrate ground must be cast before the area is altered or construction materials arrive. A structure built on unconsecrated ground deteriorates irreversibly; the structure also has a cumulative 1% chance per year of actually collapsing. A consecrated graveyard turns undead each round as a 3rd-level cleric; if an evil cleric consecrates it, undead there are instead treated as protected and controlled by an evil 3rd-level cleric.

Anathematize brands an offender with a religious identifying mark. If the subject is undeserving, the spell fails; a successful atonement makes the mark fade and may remove it. The brand disappears entirely when the offense was caused by magic or another external force, but a naturally caused offense cannot be completely removed.
conditions: Except for anathematize, no saving throw is called for: the recipient is inanimate or presumed willing. Any ceremony other than anathematize simply fails if cast on an unwilling person.

Special vows are received before the intended cavalier or paladin begins that career; the protection lasts through the upper limit of the recipient’s current level and can be renewed as described in the effect.
Consecrate ground has no effect if cast after the site has been altered or construction materials have been brought there.
exceptions: An unwilling subject of anathematize receives a save versus spell at −4. Standard service costs are: coming of age 5–15 sp; burial 5–50 gp; marriage 1–20 gp; dedication 1–10 sp (sometimes free); investiture 1–100 gp (sometimes free); consecrate item usually free; ordination usually free but possibly up to 200 gp; special vows 1–100 gp (sometimes free); consecrate ground 100–600 gp depending on area and cleric level; anathematize is performed without charge.

spells.name: Ceremony

fields.Materials: Mistletoe; a grove or healthy natural forest setting

effect: The spell leaves no aura of magic, though know alignment or similar magic may reveal the force of true neutrality involved. The source lists coming of age, rest eternal, and marriage at druid level 1; dedication and investiture at level 3; initiation and special vows at level 7; hallowed ground at level 9; and cast out at level 12. Its general sentence says each can be cast by a druid of the indicated or lower level; the initiation paragraph separately gives a rite-specific performer and timing rule.

Coming of age is usually performed when the recipient reaches age 14 and grants the same +1 bonus to one saving throw as the cleric rite. Rest eternal hastens the deceased’s spirit toward its final resting place; raise dead and resurrection cannot restore that subject, though wish can. Marriage is essentially identical to clerical ceremony.

Dedication admits a true-neutral recipient to the druid’s followers/worshipers and charges the recipient, as a druid, to preserve and protect nature and the world’s balance. Investiture must occur before the character becomes an Aspirant (1st-level druid) and conveys no other benefit.

Initiation grants the shape-changing and woodland-charm-immunity powers that become available at 7th level. It must be performed immediately after the druid begins advancing through 7th level; if performed earlier it does not work, and those powers remain unavailable until initiation.

Special vows operate like the clerical ceremony, but do not work on paladins and do work on cavaliers of any alignment. Hallowed ground is cast on the druid’s permanent grove, ensorcelling its trees against disease and other natural disasters. The ground remains hallowed while the druid maintains that grove as a permanent base.

Cast out is a severe excommunication or punishment for sacrilege against the natural environment or violation of druidic standards. The subject exudes a powerful negative aura that makes natural creatures react negatively, including normal animals, woodland monsters, domestic beasts, druids, and their followers.
conditions: A ceremony is performed in a druid grove or another natural, healthy patch of forest; mistletoe is always a material component. Rites are normally conducted at dawn or dusk.

Dedication requires true neutrality. Initiation is normally performed by another druid of 7th or higher level; in unusual cases the recipient may cast it on themself. Preserve both this rite-specific instruction and the source’s separate general indicated-or-lower-level sentence.

Cast out requires permission up the druidic hierarchy: a druid asks the Archdruid, an Archdruid asks the Great Druid, and the Great Druid asks the Grand Druid. The Grand Druid needs no permission, though a Hierophant Druid may reverse the Grand Druid’s action. The ceremony is normally reserved for serious offenses; an unwilling recipient saves versus spell at −4.
exceptions: Cast out’s effects can be lessened by a reversed ceremony cast by the same druid or another druid at least as high level as the original caster, but only a Hierophant Druid can completely cancel it. Higher-ranking druids may punish a druid who was denied permission or whose action is later reversed.

spells.name: Magic Mirror

fields.Materials: Silver mirror worth at least 1,000 gp; hawk/eagle/roc eye, nitric acid, copper and zinc
fields.Scrying detection: Check each round. The DMG states an Intelligence 12+ minimum, but its spell-user detection table contains lower-Intelligence entries; how these interact is unresolved. For non-spell-users, base chances are fighter 2%, paladin 6%, ranger 4%, thief 6%, assassin 5%, monk 1%, bard 3%; UA adds cavalier 5% and barbarian 1%. Add 1% per experience level and cumulative Intelligence bonuses above 12: 13–18 give +1%, +3%, +6%, +10%, +15%, +21% respectively. Treat monsters as the most applicable class. Spell-users use the detection-of-invisibility table instead.

effect: Makes a crystal-ball-like scrying mirror. Comprehend languages, read magic, tongues, infravision and ultravision work through it.
Detect magic, detect good/evil, message and detect illusion work with a 5% chance/caster level.
conditions: The mirror survives, unlike the other material components.
exceptions: Targets can detect scrying under crystal-ball rules; cavaliers have a base 5% chance and barbarians 1%, as noted here.

spells.name: Ensnarement

fields.Materials: A prepared protective circle, thaumaturgic triangle, or pentagram; optional special pigments or permanent inlay as described.

effect: Lures a named extraplanar creature through an apparent planar opening, intending to confine it until it agrees to one service.

The creature detects the trap on a 3d6 roll at or below its intelligence. Subtract its intelligence advantage over the caster from the roll, or add the caster's advantage. A successful check makes it ignore the opening.
A captive that agrees to serve returns instantly to its original plane when the single service is complete and it informs the caster.
conditions: State the creature's type, and its proper or given name if it has one.

Ensnarement itself does not prevent the captive from harming the caster. Use a magic circle for upper-plane or Astral creatures, a thaumaturgic triangle for Ethereal, Elemental, or Concordant Opposition creatures, or a pentagram for lower or infernal creatures.

A hand-drawn protection has a 20% base escape chance. An inlaid or carved design has a 10% base chance, tested only initially to establish whether it was made properly. Modify the chance by the difference between caster intelligence plus experience level and captive intelligence plus level or hit dice: subtract a caster advantage, add a captive advantage.

Special pigments costing 1,000 gp per turn of preparation reduce a hand-made design's base chance by 1% per turn, to zero before the intelligence/level adjustment. Improving a permanent design to zero base chance takes at least one full month and at least 50,000 gp beyond its ordinary cost.

The DM rates a bribe, promise, or threat from 0 to 6 and subtracts that rating from the captive's intelligence. A roll at or below its adjusted intelligence refuses service. Offers can be renewed after 24 hours; confinement reduces intelligence by 1 for each such day.
exceptions: Any break or blur in the protective inscription releases the captive automatically; even a straw crossing a line ruins it. The captive cannot itself place an object across the magical barrier.
Impossible or unreasonable commands are never accepted. A released creature may seek revenge.

fields.Materials: Diamond dust worth at least 500 gp and a bit of seashell. The reverse additionally requires a pinch of ordinary dust. The magic-user does not require mistletoe.

effect: Changes water in the selected area into powdery dust. Only liquid present when the spell is cast is affected.
Other water that contacts the dust can soak it or turn it into silty mud. Water within mixed liquids is affected, and water-containing potions are ruined.
The reverse produces water on the corresponding large scale.
Underwater, the spell opens a hole of 10 cubic feet per caster level. If enough water surrounds it, the inrush deals 1–4 damage per caster level to everyone within, without a save.
conditions: The magic-user version follows the druid spell with the magic-user header and no mistletoe.
One creature native to the Elemental Plane of Water can be affected per casting, regardless of its size or the spell's area; it receives a spell save to escape the effect.
exceptions: Ordinary living creatures are unaffected.
The underwater modification is expressly extended to the magic-user version on printed page 82.

spells.name: Torment

fields.Saving throw: Special; magic resistance and progressive spell saves
fields.Materials: A specially written scroll naming the creature's type by its secret name or naming the individual, and identifying the caster. Special inks cost at least 1,000 gp per subject hit die.

effect: Forces a captive extraplanar creature toward accepting a demanded service through increasingly painful recitation.
After the initial link, continued reading causes twinges in rounds 1–2, shooting pains in rounds 3–4, then aches and cramps in rounds 5–6.
The subject's spell-save penalties are −1, −2, −3, −4, −6, and −8 in rounds 1 through 6 respectively. Failure means agreement to the demand.

If it escapes, the subject suffers −1 initiative per two rounds of torment, to a maximum −4 at round 8. Its attack and per-die damage penalties begin at −1 after round 3, rise to −4 in round 6, then recede to −1 in round 9.
conditions: The subject must be confined in a magic circle, thaumaturgic triangle, or pentagram, and applicable magic resistance must fail.
For each intelligence point the creature has above the caster, it has a 1% chance of seizing control, pulling the caster into the prison, and carrying the caster to its own plane.
If the reading is interrupted or distracted, its chance to seize control is 5% per intelligence point.
An agreement is obeyed literally; the subject remains intensely hostile and seeks revenge.
exceptions: The source explicitly removes a penalty after round 8 but supplies no legible save-penalty values for rounds 7–8 in this passage; no values have been extrapolated.
Compare ensnarement and dolor for related confinement and coercion rules.

spells.name: Binding

fields.Saving throw: Special; see caster level and form
fields.Materials: Chanted text and gestures; materials vary, including appropriate miniature metal chains, rare soporific herbs, a diamond or corundum worth 1,000 gp per subject hit die, and a vellum likeness or carved statuette.

effect: Imprisons a lower-planar creature already held inside a restraining diagram. Choose one of six forms.
Chaining confines it with restraints that produce antipathy toward approaching creatures other than the caster; it lasts up to one year per effective caster level.
Slumber produces coma for up to one year per effective caster level. Bound slumber combines coma and chaining for up to one month per effective caster level.
Hedged prison confines it within an area until the magical hedge is broken. Metamorphosis makes all but its face or head noncorporeal until a prescribed freeing act.
Minimus containment reduces it to an inch tall or smaller and confines it within a gem or comparable prison. The last three forms radiate only a very faint magic aura.
conditions: No save applies if effective caster level is at least twice the subject's hit dice. Otherwise it receives a modified spell save; success frees it.
At most six magic-users can assist. Each assistant of 9th level or above adds one-third of that assistant's level; each assistant of levels 4–8 adds one level.
Chaining uses the ordinary save; slumber grants +1, bound slumber +2, hedged prison +3, metamorphosis +4, minimus containment +5.
Prior dolor imposes −1, prior torment −2, and the two used successively −4 on the save.

The first three forms can be renewed. After one year the captive gains a normal spell save and breaks free on success; interference that weakens chaining or slumber can also permit a normal save on renewal.
exceptions: The first three forms keep the subject within its restraining diagram.
Where the source says relative caster-level/hit-die ratio modifies an allowed save, it supplies no additional numeric ratio formula in this passage.

spells.name: Sink

fields.Area: One creature, or one object of up to 1 cubic spell-inch per caster level

effect: After four uninterrupted segments, a failed save roots the subject in place and gives it the density of the supporting surface.
The caster may stop then: the rooting expires after four turns. Continuing sinks the subject by one-quarter of its height in each of segments 5–8, until completely buried.
A sunken living subject is held unharmed in a state like stasis. Its uppermost part lies as far beneath the surface as the subject is tall.
Removing the surrounding ground breaks the spell and restores the subject, but does not raise it.
Underwater, it sinks below the river or sea floor; the containment's magic aura radiates through the water to the surface.

Dig, transmute rock to mud, and freedom can aid recovery without harming the subject.

Lower-level hues remain available after the illusionist can create higher-level colors; the caster may choose a color below their current level.
Pearly light persists for 1 round per caster level; a target that fails its save is blinded for that duration.
Ruby heat melts up to 1 cubic yard of ice. A creature that fails its save loses 1 point of Strength and Dexterity (−1 to hit and AC) for 1 round after being struck.
Flame sets combustibles within 1 foot of the target alight. Unless the target saves, it takes 2 additional fire damage, except when protected from fire by magical or natural means.
Amber blinds the target for 5–8 rounds unless it saves versus spell; cure blindness or dispel magic also negates this effect.

A successful emerald hit creates a magical stinking cloud with a 5-foot radius around the target. The target must save versus poison or be helpless; the printed note also says the target will be helpless until leaving the vapors.

Turquoise inflicts electrical damage. A target wearing ferrous metal is magnetized for 3–12 rounds unless it saves versus spell; magnetized metal sticks to other magnetized metal, and nonmagnetized ferrous metal clings until pulled free.
Sapphire paralyzes the target for 5–20 rounds unless it saves versus paralysis.
Amethyst turns the target to stone unless it saves versus petrification; even a successful save leaves it slowed for 2–8 rounds.
Ashen kills the target unless it saves versus death magic; even a successful save leaves it paralyzed for 2–5 rounds.
conditions: Requires an unobstructed path; magic resistance applies.
exceptions: The source’s special-power notes assign the individual duration, saving throw, area, and additional result to each hue; the listed spell and attack facts are summarized above. The 12th-level ashen table entry lists paralysis in its damage/effect column and death as its special power.

matrices.title: Original attack matrix: fighters, paladins, rangers, and related attackers
notes: All 210 cells of matrix I.B were checked against the supplied revised December 1979 Dungeon Masters Guide scan.
The table applies to fighters, paladins, and rangers. Bards use their highest attained fighter level, not their current bard level. Its separate level-0 column applies to halflings and humans.

A cell is the table's 20-sided-die target for the named attacker level band and opponent armor class, before resolving applicable adjustments. It is not automatically equivalent to AC-zero target minus armor class.
The original table repeats 20 in some columns, so a single linear THAC0 subtraction can disagree with it. The examples below use only cells actually legible in this scan.
Any current group convention using simple THAC0 remains a group choice; this reference does not silently replace that convention or the printed matrix.

ruleNotes.title: Missile range adjustments
ruleNotes.text: The matrix prints a −2 adjustment at medium missile range and −5 at long range.

contextLimitations: No independently reviewed field-to-region binding is recorded.

ruleNotes.title: Optional per-level fighter progression
ruleNotes.text: The DM may choose a +1 to-hit bonus at the second level within each two-level fighter band, producing the source's optional per-level progression instead of the ordinary two-level steps. Do not silently apply this option.

contextLimitations: No independently reviewed field-to-region binding is recorded.

ruleNotes.title: Certain spell adjustments change AC
ruleNotes.text: For the listed kinds of spell effects, including curse, prayer, and protection from evil, the DMG instructs the referee to adjust the relevant armor class rather than reduce the attack die result. This preserves the intended repeated-20 behavior. This note is about those spell adjustments, not a universal conversion of every modifier into AC.

contextLimitations: No independently reviewed field-to-region binding is recorded.

ruleNotes.title: Repeated 20s and a separate natural-20 option
ruleNotes.text: The DMG explains the repeated 20s as part of the printed combat-table progression. It then offers an optional amendment: second and later repeated-20 entries require a natural 20, and targets above 20 require a natural 20 plus sufficient bonus. The initial 20 entry still permits die result plus bonuses. Keep that amendment distinct from the unamended printed table; do not infer an unconditional natural-20 rule from it.

classes.name: Cleric
classes.description: Divine spellcaster with armor, healing, and the ability to turn undead. XP rows below are a partial transcription, not an automatic level award.
guidance: Requires Wisdom 9; some multiclass qualifications differ.
Check spell slots, Wisdom bonus spells, and turning ability for the new level.
After level 9, gain 2 hp per level instead of another hit die.
Level 8 followers require a qualifying place of worship; level 9 opens the stronghold option.

PHB p. 19, Table II: any armor or shield; club, flail, hammer, mace, or staff; oil is allowed. Poison is barred to non-evil clerics; an evil cleric needs referee permission. The starred weapon note includes magical weapons unless the item itself bars the class.
PHB p. 20: cleric spells must be spoken or read aloud, and clerics cannot use edged or pointed weapons.

classes.name: Druid
classes.description: A nature-focused cleric subclass with its own spells and a limited upper-level hierarchy. The PHB XP table is transcribed; rank advancement still has additional conditions.
guidance: Requires Wisdom 12 and Charisma 15; alignment is true neutral.
Level 3 adds identification, passage through overgrowth, and a new language; further levels add languages.
Level 7 adds immunity to charm from woodland-associated creatures and limited shapechanging.
Ranks 12–14 depend on vacancies or winning the specified challenge, as well as XP.

PHB p. 19, Table II: leather armor, wooden shield; club, dagger, dart, hammer, scimitar, sling, spear, or staff; oil is allowed. The poison ? is referee-dependent. The starred weapon note includes magical weapons unless the item itself bars the class.

PHB p. 21: druids cannot turn or control undead, demons, or devils. At 7th level a druid can change form up to three times per day, once per creature type (reptile, bird, or mammal); the assumed creature retains the druid’s mind. Forms range from a bullfrog, bluejay, or bat to a large snake, eagle, or black bear about twice the druid’s weight. Each change heals 10–60% of damage sustained before changing form.
PHB pp. 21, 34: druids have a separate secret tongue, in addition to the common, alignment, and other languages they know.

classes.name: Fighter
classes.description: The core martial class. PHB XP thresholds and source-supported level changes are available; unreadable mechanics remain explicit gaps.
guidance: Requires Strength 9 and Constitution 7.
Check the attacks-per-round table when reaching a new combat band.
After level 9, gain 3 hp per level instead of another hit die.
At level 9, establishing and clearing a freehold can attract men-at-arms and revenue.

PHB p. 19, Table II: any armor, shield, or weapon; oil is allowed and poison is referee-dependent. The any*** row restricts characters under 5 ft. from longbows or weapons over 12 ft., and characters under 100 lb. from heavy crossbows or pole arms over 200 gp weight (including two-handed swords).
PHB p. 22: Strength above 15 grants a 10% bonus to experience awarded. The fighter may be of any alignment.

UA p. 13 Table II lists the Fighter for any armor, shield, and weapons; oil is permitted and poison is the DM’s option. UA p. 26 lists four initial weapon proficiencies, a −2 nonproficiency penalty, and one added proficiency per three levels.

UA p. 18 allows weapon specialization only for Fighters and Rangers, chosen at character creation and costing two weapon-proficiency slots. From the initial allotment of four Fighter or three Ranger weapons, ordinary specialization leaves one specialist weapon plus two or one other proficient weapons; bow specialization (but not crossbow specialization) costs one extra slot, leaving the Fighter one other proficiency and the Ranger none. A melee specialist gains +1 to hit and +2 damage. A bow specialist has 6–30-foot point-blank range (+2 to hit and damage, double damage on a successful hit) and +1 to hit and damage at short range; the bow can be fired before initiative if the arrow is nocked, shaft drawn, and target in sight. A crossbow specialist has 6–60-foot point-blank range (+2 to hit and damage, double damage), short range +1 to hit and damage, and medium range +1 to hit only; it can fire before initiative if cocked, aimed, and the target is in range. Other missile specialists gain +1 to hit and +2 damage. Specialization hit bonuses are not magical and do not enable hits on creatures affected only by magical weapons. Use the existing UA specialization-rate table for weapon-specific rates; it supersedes ordinary rates while the specialist weapon is used.

UA p. 18 distinguishes the initial specialization choice, made when the character is created, from double specialization, which a fighter or ranger may choose initially or later for the same specific weapon type already specialized in. Double specialization is limited to melee weapons other than pole arms and the two-handed sword; it uses the proficiency slot that would otherwise gain a new weapon and grants +3 to hit and +3 damage. For ordinary melee specialization, +1 to hit and +2 damage stack with Strength and magic bonuses, and the weapon must be a specific type (for example, long sword rather than “sword”). For a crossbow specialist, the 6–60-foot point-blank category completely replaces a light crossbow’s ordinary short range in a dungeon.

classes.name: Paladin
classes.description: The PHB lawful-good fighter subclass. Keep this progression distinct from the UA cavalier-based revision.
guidance: Human only: Strength 12, Intelligence 9, Wisdom 13, Constitution 9, and Charisma 17 are required.
Level 3 adds turning at the ability of a level-1 cleric; level 4 permits calling a warhorse.
Clerical spell use begins at level 9; check the class spell table.
After level 9, gain 3 hp per level; XP does not remove alignment, tithe, or conduct requirements.

PHB p. 19, Table II: any armor, shield, or weapon; oil is allowed; poison is never allowed. The any*** row restricts characters under 5 ft. from longbows or weapons over 12 ft., and characters under 100 lb. from heavy crossbows or pole arms over 200 gp weight (including two-handed swords).

PHB pp. 22, 24: a paladin may retain at most 10 magic items (1 suit of armor, 1 shield, 4 weapons, 4 other items); a magic bow and magic arrows together count as one weapon. The paladin retains only enough wealth for a modest lifestyle, henchmen/servants, and a small castle; gives away excess and tithes 10% of all income to a lawful-good charitable religious institution, and attracts no men-at-arms.

classes.name: Ranger
classes.description: A good-aligned fighter subclass skilled in tracking, scouting, and fighting giant-class enemies.
guidance: Requires Strength 13, Intelligence 13, Wisdom 14, and Constitution 14; alignment must remain good.
The first level starts with two hit dice, rather than one.
Druidic spells begin at level 8, and magic-user spells at level 9.
At level 10, check followers and new item use; after level 10, gain 2 hp per level.

PHB p. 19, Table II: any armor, shield, or weapon; oil is allowed and poison is referee-dependent. The any*** row restricts characters under 5 ft. from longbows or weapons over 12 ft., and characters under 100 lb. from heavy crossbows or pole arms over 200 gp weight (including two-handed swords).

PHB p. 24: underground tracking requires observing the creature within 3 turns and starting at the place observed; outdoors the base chance is 90%, modified by party size, elapsed time, and precipitation. Use the separate listed action chances underground.

PHB pp. 24–25: a ranger adds one point of melee damage per experience level against listed giant-class humanoids, surprises opponents 50% of the time, and is surprised 16 2/3% of the time. No more than three rangers may operate together; level-10 followers are 2–24 and cannot be replaced.

UA p. 13 Table II lists the Ranger for any armor, shield, and weapons; oil is permitted and poison is the DM’s option. UA p. 26 lists three initial weapon proficiencies*, a −2 nonproficiency penalty, and one added proficiency per three levels; the star note restricts Ranger weapon choices.

UA p. 18 allows weapon specialization only for Fighters and Rangers, chosen at character creation and costing two weapon-proficiency slots. From the initial allotment of four Fighter or three Ranger weapons, ordinary specialization leaves one specialist weapon plus two or one other proficient weapons; bow specialization (but not crossbow specialization) costs one extra slot, leaving the Fighter one other proficiency and the Ranger none. A melee specialist gains +1 to hit and +2 damage. A bow specialist has 6–30-foot point-blank range (+2 to hit and damage, double damage on a successful hit) and +1 to hit and damage at short range; the bow can be fired before initiative if the arrow is nocked, shaft drawn, and target in sight. A crossbow specialist has 6–60-foot point-blank range (+2 to hit and damage, double damage), short range +1 to hit and damage, and medium range +1 to hit only; it can fire before initiative if cocked, aimed, and the target is in range. Other missile specialists gain +1 to hit and +2 damage. Specialization hit bonuses are not magical and do not enable hits on creatures affected only by magical weapons. Use the existing UA specialization-rate table for weapon-specific rates; it supersedes ordinary rates while the specialist weapon is used.

UA pp. 21–22 add situation-specific tracking procedures to the Ranger’s level-by-level base chances already recorded in this class entry. Outdoors, the base is 10% per level plus 10%, with a 110% base ceiling; terrain, group size, crossing/overtracking, trail age, precipitation, and deliberate concealment modify the attempt. Indoor tracking uses separate surface categories, the same base and specified shared modifiers, and additional observation prerequisites; movement rate depends on track clarity and illumination. Apply the printed definitions and impossibility limits, and keep the p. 22 identification roll separate from the tracking roll.
UA p. 21 distinguishes the outdoor base-chance ceiling of 110% from the final adjusted chance: after modifiers, an adjusted chance above 100% is treated as 100%.

UA p. 18 distinguishes the initial specialization choice, made when the character is created, from double specialization, which a fighter or ranger may choose initially or later for the same specific weapon type already specialized in. Double specialization is limited to melee weapons other than pole arms and the two-handed sword; it uses the proficiency slot that would otherwise gain a new weapon and grants +3 to hit and +3 damage. For ordinary melee specialization, +1 to hit and +2 damage stack with Strength and magic bonuses, and the weapon must be a specific type (for example, long sword rather than “sword”). For a crossbow specialist, the 6–60-foot point-blank category completely replaces a light crossbow’s ordinary short range in a dungeon.

classes.name: Magic-user
classes.description: An arcane spellcaster who learns and prepares spells from spellbooks. The PHB XP table is transcribed; individual progression mechanics remain incomplete.
guidance: Requires Intelligence 9 and Dexterity 6; Intelligence limits spell learning and access.
Check new spell slots and the spellbook needed for newly available spell levels.
After level 11, gain 1 hp per level instead of another hit die.
At level 11, enchanting items and inscribing magic scrolls become possible; a cleared stronghold is possible from level 12. Separate procedures apply.

PHB p. 19, Table II: no armor or shield; dagger, dart, or staff; oil is allowed and poison is referee-dependent. The starred weapon note includes magical weapons unless the item itself bars the class.

PHB p. 25: a cast spell must be regained by consulting its proper spellbook before it can be cast again; all spells must be spoken or read aloud. Spellbooks must be maintained as new spells become usable.

classes.name: Illusionist
classes.description: A magic-user subclass with its own spell list, item permissions, and advancement table.
guidance: Requires Intelligence 15 and Dexterity 16; high scores grant no XP bonus for this class.
Use the illusionist spell-slot table and spell list rather than the magic-user equivalents.
After level 10, gain 1 hp per level instead of another hit die.
At level 10 and above, the source permits manufacturing suitable magic items; separate procedures apply.

PHB p. 19, Table II: no armor or shield; dagger, dart, or staff; oil is allowed and poison is referee-dependent. The starred weapon note includes magical weapons unless the item itself bars the class.
PHB p. 26: use the Illusionist-specific magic-item permissions; the listed magic-user scrolls are usable only when they contain spells the Illusionist can use.

classes.name: Assassin
classes.description: A thief subclass focused on assassination, disguise, and spying; higher guild ranks require more than an XP total.
guidance: Requires Strength 12, Intelligence 11, and Dexterity 12; high abilities grant no XP bonus.
Most thieving functions are performed two levels below assassin level; backstab is an exception.
At level 9 and above, Intelligence 15+ can permit additional alignment languages.
Advancing beyond level 13 requires defeating the current guild leader; level 15 has a further leadership challenge.

PHB p. 19, Table II: leather armor, any shield or weapon; oil and poison are allowed. The any*** row restricts characters under 5 ft. from longbows or weapons over 12 ft., and characters under 100 lb. from heavy crossbows or pole arms over 200 gp weight (including two-handed swords).

PHB p. 29: poison placement and timing must be specified for the referee to adjudicate, and a poisoned weapon may be noticed. The minimum-fee table is keyed by assassin level and victim-level bracket; important, popular, or noble victims may count above actual level. Fees are separate from XP awards.

classes.name: Monk
classes.description: A martial discipline with open-hand combat, level-based abilities, and limited higher ranks. The PHB XP table is transcribed.
guidance: Verify the demanding entry requirements in the source before choosing this class.
Update armor class, open-hand combat, and special abilities; PHB p. 30 and DMG p. 74 disagree on the monk attack table, so confirm the campaign ruling.
Level 6 permits limited henchmen; level 8 begins the restricted higher ranks.
Level 8 and above requires a successful unarmed challenge for a rank, as well as sufficient XP.

PHB p. 19, Table II: no armor or shield; bo sticks, club, crossbow, dagger, hand axe, javelin, jo stick, pole arm, spear, or staff; oil is not allowed and poison is referee-dependent. The starred weapon note includes magical weapons unless the item itself bars the class.

PHB p. 30: open-hand attacks can stun or kill. A stun requires a hit roll at least 5 above the minimum required and lasts 1–6 melee rounds. Killing is a separate percentile roll: the monk must first hit and stun, then roll equal to or below the opponent’s AC modified by the monk’s levels above 7; the source notes a negative chance at AC −1.

PHB p. 32: quivering palm is a separate ability, attempted only once per week; the monk must touch the intended victim within 3 melee rounds or the power is drained for one week. It has no effect on undead or creatures hit only by magical weapons; the victim cannot have more hit dice than the monk, and its hit points cannot exceed the monk’s by more than 200%. The death command must come within one day per monk level at use or the vibrations cease harmlessly. The general monk restriction is no Strength bonus to hit probability or damage.
